title: Two Sum — return indices of pair summing to target (HashMap of complement).
shortTitle: Two Sum — Return Indices of a Pair Summing to Target

s1_definition.profdef: The Two Sum problem asks for the indices of two elements in an array that add up to a given target. The efficient solution scans the array once, and for each element computes the complement, which is the target minus the current value, then checks a HashMap that maps already-seen values to their indices; if the complement is present, you have the pair, otherwise you store the current value and index and continue. This runs in average linear time, far better than the quadratic brute-force double loop.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India wants to find two transactions on Rajesh's account that together make up a suspicious round figure, say a target amount flagged by the fraud rules. Instead of comparing every transaction against every other, a clerk walks the list once holding a notebook of amounts already seen and where they were. For each new transaction the clerk works out how much would be needed to reach the target and checks the notebook; if that complement is already noted, the pair is found. One pass, with a quick notebook lookup each time.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each value, look up target minus value in a HashMap of seen values; a hit is the answer, otherwise record the value and move on.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Two Sum problem asks for the indices of two elements in an array that add up to a given target. The efficient solution scans the array once, and for each element computes the complement, which is the target minus the current value, then checks a HashMap that maps already-seen values to their indices; if the complement is present, you have the pair, otherwise you store the current value and index and continue. This runs in average linear time, far better than the quadratic brute-force double loop.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India wants to find two transactions on Rajesh's account that together make up a suspicious round figure, say a target amount flagged by the fraud rules. Instead of comparing every transaction against every other, a clerk walks the list once holding a notebook of amounts already seen and where they were. For each new transaction the clerk works out how much would be needed to reach the target and checks the notebook; if that complement is already noted, the pair is found. One pass, with a quick notebook lookup each time.

**One line to remember:** For each value, look up target minus value in a HashMap of seen values; a hit is the answer, otherwise record the value and move on.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute-force approach uses two nested loops, checking every pair, which is quadratic time. That is fine for tiny arrays but far too slow for large ones. The HashMap approach turns it into a single pass by trading memory for speed.

You create a HashMap whose keys are values you have already seen and whose values are the indices where you saw them. You loop once. For the current element at index i, you compute the complement as target minus the current value. You ask the map whether it contains the complement. If it does, the stored index for that complement together with the current index i form the answer, so you return them. If it does not, you put the current value and its index into the map and continue to the next element.

The order matters: you check for the complement before you insert the current value. This naturally avoids pairing an element with itself, because the current value is not yet in the map when you look for its complement. If you inserted first and then checked, an element whose value is exactly half the target could wrongly match itself.

This is average linear time because each map lookup and insert is average constant time and you do one per element. The extra space is linear for the map. For sorted input there is an alternative two-pointer approach that uses constant extra space by moving a left and right pointer inward, but it requires the array to be sorted, which either costs N log N or loses the original indices, so when the problem asks for original indices on unsorted data the HashMap approach is the right choice.

A senior point is handling the finance data types and duplicates. For money I use BigDecimal keys and compareTo-consistent equality, being mindful of the scale trap, so I normalise scale when building keys. If the same value appears twice and the target is twice that value, the map must hold the first occurrence so the second occurrence finds it; checking before inserting makes this work correctly.

Another senior point is what to return when no pair exists. I prefer returning an empty or optional result rather than a sentinel like negative one that a caller might misuse, and I document that only the first found pair is returned unless the requirement asks for all pairs, in which case I continue scanning and collect them.

A small finance-domain example: `Map<BigDecimal,Integer> seen = new HashMap<>(); for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { BigDecimal need = target.subtract(a[i]); Integer j = seen.get(need); if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i}; seen.put(a[i], i); }` returns the index pair summing to target.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India fraud engine flags round-figure targets, and it needs to know whether any two transactions on Rajesh's account add up exactly to a flagged target, because a split-into-two pattern is a known evasion trick. The engine must find such a pair fast across a long list and report where the two transactions are. Finding the index pair with the HashMap complement technique is exactly this.

This is exactly how Two Sum works in Java — for each transaction we look up the complement amount in a map of amounts already seen.

Problem 2 — Amounts are BigDecimal and numerically equal values may carry different scale, so the map keys must be normalised so that a complement is found even when scales differ, and the engine must return a clear empty result when no such pair exists rather than a confusing sentinel. This shows the data-type care and the clean no-result contract.

What the code will do: a `FraudPairFinder` with `findPairSummingTo(BigDecimal[] amounts, BigDecimal target)` using a HashMap of normalised amounts to indices, checking the complement before inserting, and returning an Optional pair. The demo finds a pair that hits the target and confirms a clean empty result when none exists.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the amounts are `30000, 5000, 70000.00, 12000` and the target is `100000`.

Step 1: We create a HashMap pre-sized to twice the length. At index zero the value is `30000`. The complement is `100000 - 30000 = 70000`. The map is empty, so there is no complement yet. We put the normalised `30000` with index zero into the map.

Step 2: At index one the value is `5000`. The complement is `95000`. The map does not contain `95000`, so we put `5000` with index one into the map.

Step 3: At index two the value is `70000.00`. We normalise it, and the complement is `100000 - 70000.00 = 30000`, also normalised. We look up `30000` in the map.

Step 4: The map contains `30000` at index zero. That is a hit: indices zero and two together sum to the target. We return the pair zero and two immediately. Because the stored key was the normalised form, the scale difference between `70000.00` and the stored `30000` did not prevent the match.

Step 5: The demo logs the suspicious pair, showing `30000` at index zero plus `70000.00` at index two equals the flagged `100000`. The fraud engine now knows exactly which two transactions form the split pattern.

Step 6: For the target `999999`, no complement is ever found as we scan, so the loop completes and the method returns an empty Optional. The demo reports that no pair is present, using a clean empty result rather than a sentinel value.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T17:10:00Z INFO Pair found at indices 0 and 2 summing to Rs.100000
2026-10-26T17:10:00Z INFO FRAUD CHECK: indices 0+2 = Rs.30000 + Rs.70000.00
2026-10-26T17:10:00Z INFO No pair sums to Rs.999999
2026-10-26T17:10:00Z INFO Pair for 999999 present? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [30000, 5000, 70000.00, 12000], target=100000
    │
    ▼
  HashMap seen (value → index)
    │ i0 30000: need 70000 — miss → put 30000@0
    │ i1 5000 : need 95000 — miss → put 5000@1
    │ i2 70000: need 30000 — HIT at index 0 → return {0,2}
    ▼
  pair indices {0, 2}
    │
    ├─ target 999999: every complement misses → Optional.empty()
    ▼
  Output: fraud pair located; clean empty when none
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Two Sum asks for the indices of two elements that add up to a target, and the efficient solution is a single pass with a HashMap from value to index. For each element I compute the complement, which is the target minus the current value, and I check whether that complement is already in the map; if it is, the stored index and the current index are the answer, otherwise I record the current value and index and move on. It is average linear time, which beats the quadratic brute-force double loop.

The ordering detail that keeps it correct is that I check for the complement before inserting the current value. That way an element is never paired with itself, which would otherwise happen when a value is exactly half the target. If the same value legitimately appears twice and the target is twice that value, checking before inserting also lets the second occurrence find the first.

I note the alternative: on sorted data a two-pointer approach uses constant extra space, but it needs sorting, which costs N log N or loses the original indices, so when the problem wants original indices on unsorted data the HashMap approach is the right default. For money I use BigDecimal keys and normalise scale, because BigDecimal equals considers scale and would otherwise miss a numerically equal complement, and I return an Optional rather than a sentinel when no pair exists.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the fraud engine to detect a split-into-two evasion pattern, finding whether any two transactions on Rajesh's account add up exactly to a flagged round-figure target and reporting which two. Amounts are BigDecimal with possible scale differences, so I normalise the keys, and I return a clean empty result when no pair is found. Explaining the complement trick, the check-before-insert ordering, and the BigDecimal normalisation shows the interviewer that I know the optimal approach and the real data pitfalls.
